question: When performing the Straight Leg Raise (SLR) test in a patient with suspected L5–S1 disc herniation, which finding most specifically indicates nerve root tension?

answers.text: Reproduction of pain in the low back when the leg is raised beyond 80°

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Back pain alone on SLR is non-specific and can result from lumbar muscle or sacroiliac stretch. Root tension requires pain to radiate below the knee.

answers.text: Reproduction of pain radiating below the knee (along the sciatic distribution) at 30–70° of hip flexion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A positive SLR requires sciatica (pain below the knee in the dermatomal distribution) reproduced between 30° and 70°. Pain appearing only above 70° or confined to the back does not meet the tension-sign criterion.

answers.text: Tight hamstrings causing the patient to flex the knee to relieve discomfort during leg raising

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hamstring tightness is the commonest cause of false-positive SLR discomfort; it does not reproduce true radicular pain below the knee.

answers.text: Reproduction of pain at the site of the disc herniation in the lumbar spine at any angle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Localised lumbar pain on SLR is not a positive root tension sign. The key feature is dermatomal pain radiating below the knee.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: SLR is positive only when the movement reproduces radiating pain BELOW the knee in the sciatic distribution, typically between 30° and 70° of hip flexion. Back pain alone or hamstring tightness does not constitute a positive sign.

Well done. Positive SLR = dermatomal pain below the knee at 30–70°. The crossed SLR (pain in the affected leg when the opposite leg is raised) is even more specific for large central/paracentral herniations.
